title: 22. Interview: TTL (Time To Live)
summary: Interview Q&A for TTL (Time To Live) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 TTL (Time To Live) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is a TTL, and why is it the foundation of cache consistency?
**Answer:** A TTL (Time To Live) is a per-entry deadline attached to a cached value: after the deadline, the entry is considered stale and is either re-fetched or served conditionally as stale. TTL is the foundation of cache consistency because it provides the only self-cleaning mechanism that doesn't require explicit invalidation: every entry is guaranteed to be evicted (or refreshed) within at most `TTL` seconds of being written, regardless of whether anyone touches it. Without TTL, a cache can serve stale data forever — until LRU/LFU evicts the entry under memory pressure, which may never happen if the cache isn't full. With TTL, the operator has a hard upper bound on staleness ("users see data at most 60 seconds old"), which is the contract that makes caching safe for data that changes in the source. TTL composes with capacity-based eviction (LRU/LFU): the entry is evicted when its TTL expires OR when LRU/LFU picks it, whichever comes first. Real-world: every caching layer in production uses TTL — DNS (A records), HTTP (Cache-Control: max-age), Redis (EXPIRE), Memcached (set's third arg), CDNs (edge TTLs). Without TTL, none of these would have a correctness story.
**Visual:**
```
Without TTL:
  T=0 write K=V    T=1000s source changes V->V'
  T=2000s read K   -> still V (stale, no bound)
  + staleness unbounded, depends on LRU eviction

With TTL=60s:
  T=0 write K=V, expires_at=60
  T=30 read K -> V (fresh)
  T=61 read K -> miss, fetch V' from source, re-store
  + staleness bounded at <= 60s
```

### Q2. What is the freshness-vs-load trade-off in choosing a TTL?
**Answer:** The TTL value controls the freshness-vs-load dial directly. A short TTL (e.g., 5 seconds) means cached data is at most 5 seconds old — very fresh — but the cache absorbs little load: every key that's accessed more than once per 5 seconds misses each window, and the backend sees a steady stream of refreshes (low hit rate). A long TTL (e.g., 1 hour) means cached data may be up to 1 hour stale — less fresh — but the cache absorbs most of the load: a key accessed every 10 seconds hits 360 times before expiring, so hit rate is 99.7% and the backend is protected. The right value depends on the cost of staleness and the cost of the backend call. For a banking balance (staleness costs money/trust), pick a short TTL or no cache at all. For a product image (staleness costs nothing), pick a long TTL. For a moderately-sensitive value like a user profile, pick a compromise (5–60 seconds) and use stale-while-revalidate to mask the refresh latency. Operators typically pick the longest TTL that keeps staleness under the application's tolerance, then measure hit rate and backend QPS to confirm. Real-world: Stripe uses a 24-hour TTL for idempotency keys (immutable, no staleness concern); Netflix uses 30 seconds for watch progress (user-visible freshness); GitHub uses 5 minutes for rendered README HTML (compromise).
**Visual:**
```
TTL choice on the freshness-vs-load dial:

  short TTL (5s)            long TTL (1h)
  +---------------+-------------+
  fresh <--------  |  --------> load-protected
  |
  v
  hit rate low (refreshes every 5s)
  backend QPS high
  staleness low

  right TTL = longest value that keeps staleness acceptable
  + use SWR to mask refresh latency
```

### Q3. What is the thundering herd problem, and how does TTL jitter prevent it?
**Answer:** The thundering herd (or cache stampede) happens when many cached entries expire at the same instant and thousands of concurrent requests miss simultaneously, all hitting the backend at once. The classic trigger: a popular key is written with TTL=60 at T=0; over the next minute, thousands of clients read it (hits); at T=60 the key expires; the next 1,000 concurrent requests all miss, all fetch from the backend, and all try to repopulate the cache. If the backend fetch takes 200 ms and the request rate is 10,000 QPS, 2,000 requests pile up at the backend before the cache is repopulated — potentially overwhelming it. TTL jitter prevents this by adding randomness: instead of TTL=60, write TTL=60 + random(0, 10). The expirations now spread across a 10-second window, so refreshes trickle rather than herd — at most a few refreshes per second instead of thousands at T=60. Jitter is the cheapest stampede defense: no coordination between clients, no extra infrastructure, no latency cost. Real-world: Cloudflare adds up to 10% jitter to all CDN TTLs to prevent synchronized re-fetches across POPs; Netflix's EVCache injects jitter into every TTL to avoid herd re-warming after deploys; AWS ElastiCache documents the pattern. The remaining herd (within the jitter window) is handled by singleflight or probabilistic early refresh (Topic 12).
**Visual:**
```
Without jitter (TTL=60s exactly):
  T=0    T=60.000  T=60.001  T=60.200
   |       |         |          |
   write -- 1000 reqs all miss  cache repopulated
            v
            DB: 1000 simultaneous queries (herd!)

With jitter (TTL=60 + random(0,10)):
  T=0    T=62    T=64    T=66    T=68    T=70
   |      |       |       |       |       |
   write  miss    miss    miss    miss    miss
          1 req   1 req   1 req   1 req   1 req
          v       v       v       v       v
          DB: 1 query each, spread over 10s (no herd)
```

### Q4. What is stale-while-revalidate (SWR), and how does it improve on plain TTL?
**Answer:** Stale-while-revalidate (SWR) uses TTL as a soft signal rather than a hard cutoff. An entry has two TTLs: a fresh TTL (the value is definitely fresh) and a stale TTL (the value may be stale but is still served while a background refresh happens). On read: if now < fresh TTL, serve fresh; if fresh TTL < now < stale TTL, serve the stale value AND trigger an asynchronous background refresh; if now > stale TTL, miss synchronously. SWR gives the best of both worlds: the freshness of a short TTL with the load reduction of a long TTL, because the background refresh hides the backend latency from the user. Concretely, with `max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600`, the cache serves fresh responses for 60 seconds, then serves stale responses (with a background refresh) for another 600 seconds — the user never waits for a refresh unless the key hasn't been accessed in 10 minutes. SWR also eliminates the thundering herd within the stale window: only one background refresh runs (the cache deduplicates refreshes via a singleflight-style lock), and other readers get the stale value immediately. Real-world: HTTP's `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` is supported by Cloudflare, Fastly, and Varnish; React Query and SWR (the library) implement it client-side; Caffeine supports it server-side via `refreshAfterWrite`.
**Visual:**
```
SWR timeline (max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600):

  T=0    T=60        T=660
   |      |            |
   write  fresh ends   stale ends
   |      |            |
   v      v            v
   FRESH  STALE+REFRESH  HARD MISS
   serve  serve stale,   sync refresh,
   fresh  bg refresh     user waits
   (0ms)  (0ms + bg)     (~200ms)

  user-perceived latency: 0ms in fresh AND stale windows
  backend hit rate: same as long TTL (1 refresh per 660s)
```

### Q5. What is the difference between lazy and active expiration, and why does Redis use both?
**Answer:** Lazy expiration checks an entry's deadline only when the entry is read: on every GET, the cache compares the deadline to now and, if expired, treats it as a miss and evicts it. Active expiration runs a background sweep that periodically scans for expired entries and evicts them proactively, regardless of whether they're being read. Lazy expiration is cheap in CPU (no background work) but can leak memory: expired entries that are never read again sit in memory until LRU/LFU evicts them under pressure. Active expiration reclaims memory promptly but costs CPU for the sweep. Redis uses both: a background task runs every 100 ms (`hz=10`), samples up to 20 expired keys, and evicts them; on every read, it also checks the deadline and evicts-on-read if expired. The combination gives correctness (lazy check guarantees no stale reads) and memory hygiene (active sweep reclaims expired entries that aren't being read). Redis's `active-expire-effort` (1–10) controls sweep aggressiveness: higher values sample more keys per sweep, reclaiming memory faster but using more CPU. Memcached is purely lazy — expired entries sit until accessed or evicted. Real-world: Redis operators tune `hz` and `active-expire-effort` based on the workload; if many short-TTL keys are written and never read again, raising `active-expire-effort` prevents memory bloat.
**Visual:**
```
Lazy expiration (Memcached, Redis on-read):
  T=0  write K=V, expires_at=60
  T=60 entry expires (but still in memory)
  T=120 read K -> check expires_at, evict, miss
  + between T=60 and T=120: stale entry wastes memory

Active expiration (Redis background sweep):
  T=0  write K=V, expires_at=60
  T=60.1 sweep samples K, sees expired, evicts
  + memory reclaimed promptly
  - CPU spent on sweep

Redis: both
  + active sweep hz=10/s (reclaims memory)
  + lazy check on read   (guarantees correctness)
  + active-expire-effort 1-10 tunes aggressiveness
```

### Q6. How does TTL interact with capacity-based eviction (LRU/LFU)?
**Answer:** TTL and capacity-based eviction (LRU/LFU) are complementary, not alternative — most production caches apply both. TTL provides a freshness bound: every entry is evicted within at most `TTL` seconds of being written, guaranteeing an upper bound on staleness. LRU/LFU provides a memory bound: when the cache fills, the least valuable entry (least recently or least frequently used) is evicted to make room. The two compose: an entry is evicted when its TTL expires OR when LRU/LFU picks it as a victim, whichever comes first. Without TTL, an LRU/LFU-only cache can serve stale data forever (until evicted), which is wrong for data that changes in the source. Without LRU/LFU, a TTL-only cache with a long TTL and a high write rate will eventually evict everything via memory pressure (using FIFO or random eviction, which has poor hit rate). The combination gives both freshness and good hit rate. Real-world: Redis deployments almost always combine `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` (or lfu) with per-key EXPIRE; Memcached combines LRU with per-key expiration; CDNs combine Cache-Control max-age with capacity-based eviction at the POP. The one nuance: in Redis, an expired key (deadline passed but not yet evicted by the sweep) is still subject to LRU eviction — so the LRU sample may include expired keys, which the lazy check evicts on contact.
**Visual:**
```
Two eviction triggers, whichever fires first:

  +----------------------+
  | Entry K=V            |
  | written at T=0       |
  | TTL=60s              |  <-- trigger 1: TTL expires at T=60
  | last accessed T=5    |
  +----------------------+
            |
            v
  evicted when:
    (a) TTL expires (T=60), OR
    (b) LRU picks K as victim (if cache full and K is oldest)

  Without TTL:   only (b), staleness unbounded
  Without LRU:   only (a), poor hit rate under memory pressure
  Both:          freshness + good hit rate (production default)
```

### Q7. When would you use a per-key TTL vs a per-class (namespace) TTL?
**Answer:** Per-key TTL means every write specifies its own TTL — flexible but error-prone, because the application has to know the right TTL for every key. Per-class TTL groups keys by namespace (e.g., `user:123`, `product:456`) and assigns a default TTL per class — simpler, because operators change one number per class rather than auditing every SET. Per-key TTL is right when keys in the same namespace have genuinely different freshness requirements: e.g., a `session:abc` key with TTL=300 (5 minutes) for an active user, but TTL=30 for a session that's been idle (the application knows the user's activity level). Per-class TTL is right when keys in a namespace share freshness requirements: e.g., all `product:*` keys should expire every 5 minutes, all `config:*` keys every 60 seconds, all `image:*` keys every 1 day. Most production deployments use per-class TTL as the default, with per-key overrides for special cases. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache configures per-app TTLs in a central property file (operators change one number per app); Discord configures per-namespace TTLs in their Redis proxy; Redis operators use the key-prefix convention to map prefixes to TTL policies enforced at the application layer. Per-class TTL is also easier to audit: a single config file documents the TTL policy for every namespace, vs hunting through code for every SET call.
**Visual:**
```
Per-key TTL (flexible, error-prone):
  SET user:123 V EX 300     # each call specifies TTL
  SET user:456 V EX 60      # different TTL per call
  + flexible
  - operator must audit every SET to know policy

Per-class TTL (simple, auditable):
  config file:
    user:*   -> 300s
    product:* -> 300s
    config:* -> 60s
    image:*  -> 86400s
  application: SET user:123 V   (TTL applied by class)
  + one place to change policy
  + easy to audit
  - less flexible (all user:* keys share TTL)

Production default: per-class with per-key overrides for special cases
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run a news site. The homepage is cached for 60 seconds. When a breaking story is published, users complain it doesn't appear for up to a minute. How do you fix this without sacrificing the cache hit rate?
**Answer:** Use a shorter TTL with stale-while-revalidate, plus an event-driven invalidation for breaking stories. Concretely: set the homepage cache to `max-age=10, stale-while-revalidate=600`. Now users see content at most 10 seconds old (vs 60 previously), but the cache still absorbs 99% of reads because the SWR window serves stale values while refreshing in the background — hit rate stays high. For breaking stories specifically, add an event-driven purge: when the CMS publishes a breaking story, it sends a `PURGE /homepage` request to the CDN (or `DEL homepage` to Redis), which evicts the cached entry immediately. The next request refreshes from the origin and sees the new story. This combines the cheapness of TTL (no invalidation needed for routine updates) with the freshness of explicit invalidation (for breaking news). Real-world: The New York Times and The Guardian use CDN purge APIs for breaking news; Cloudflare, Fastly, and Akamai all support instant purge; the BBC's homepage cache uses a 30-second TTL with a manual purge for major stories. The pattern generalizes: TTL for routine freshness, explicit invalidation for must-be-instant updates.
**Visual:**
```
Before (TTL=60s, no purge):
  T=0  publish story    T=60 cache expires   T=61 story appears
  users wait up to 60s

After (max-age=10, SWR=600, + purge on breaking):
  T=0    publish story, send PURGE
  T=0.1  CDN evicts homepage
  T=0.2  next request refreshes -> story appears
  users see story within ~200ms

  routine updates: TTL=10s + SWR=600s (hit rate ~99%)
  breaking news:   explicit PURGE (instant)
```

### Q2. Your Redis cache has 100M keys, 80% with TTLs of 1–5 seconds. Memory keeps growing despite the short TTLs. What's happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The likely cause is that Redis's active expiration sweep can't keep up with the rate of expiring keys, so expired-but-not-yet-swept entries accumulate in memory. Redis's sweep runs every 100 ms (`hz=10`) and samples up to 20 keys per sweep by default — that's at most 200 keys/s of active eviction, far below the rate at which 100M short-TTL keys expire. The fix has two parts. (1) Raise the active-expire aggressiveness: set `hz 100` (sweep every 10 ms) and `active-expire-effort 10` (maximum aggressiveness, samples more keys per sweep and runs longer). This typically 10x's the eviction throughput. (2) If that's not enough, raise `maxmemory` and set `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` so that LRU evicts expired-but-unswept entries under memory pressure — the lazy check on read will evict them on contact anyway, but LRU prevents memory bloat in the meantime. Long-term, reconsider whether 100M 1–5-second TTL keys is the right design: short TTLs on a huge key space produce massive write churn and expiration churn, and the cache provides little value (hit rate is low because keys expire before being re-accessed). Consider aggregating the data (fewer, larger keys with longer TTLs) or using a different store (e.g., a time-series DB for ephemeral metrics). Real-world: Redis operators hit this when using Redis as a rate-limiter counter store; the fix is `hz 100` + `active-expire-effort 10`, and often a redesign to use sliding-window logs instead of per-key counters.
**Visual:**
```
Problem:
  100M keys, 80% with TTL 1-5s
  expiration rate: ~20M keys/s expiring
  Redis sweep: hz=10, samples 20/sweep = 200 evictions/s
  + sweep can't keep up, expired entries accumulate
  + memory grows despite short TTLs

Fix:
  (1) hz 100, active-expire-effort 10
      -> sweep every 10ms, samples more keys
      -> eviction throughput ~10x
  (2) maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
      -> LRU evicts expired-but-unswept under pressure
      -> lazy check on read evicts on contact

Long-term:
  + short TTL on huge key space = low hit rate + high churn
  + redesign: aggregate data, fewer/longer-TTL keys
```

### Q3. Your team deployed a new version of the user-profile service. After deploy, the cache still serves old profile data for up to 5 minutes (the TTL). Users see stale data. How do you prevent this on future deploys?
**Answer:** Two complementary fixes. (1) **Versioned cache keys**: include the deploy version in the cache key — `user:123:v42` instead of `user:123`. On deploy, the new code reads `user:123:v43`, which misses (no such key), fetches fresh data, and populates the new key. The old keys (`:v42`) expire naturally via TTL or are evicted by LRU. This is the cleanest fix because it requires no coordination between deploy and cache. (2) **Deploy-triggered flush**: on deploy, the deploy pipeline sends a `FLUSHDB` (or pattern-based `DEL user:*`) to the cache, evicting all old entries. The next reads miss and fetch fresh data. This is simpler but causes a brief spike in backend load (every key misses at once — a cache stampede, mitigated by warming the cache before cutting traffic over). The combination is best: versioned keys for routine deploys (no flush needed, no stampede), with an optional flush for emergency rollbacks. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache uses versioned keys per deploy (the deploy ID is part of the key prefix); Stripe includes a schema version in cache keys so a schema change invalidates automatically; Facebook's TAO uses a "version" field in the cache key for the same reason. The pattern generalizes: any change to the shape or semantics of cached data should bump the key version, not rely on TTL expiring the old data.
**Visual:**
```
Problem (no versioning):
  deploy v42 -> v43 (same cache key user:123)
  T=0    deploy, code expects new data shape
  T=0    cache still has user:123 = old data, TTL=300s
  T=0-300  users see stale data until TTL expires

Fix 1: versioned cache keys
  v42 code: GET user:123:v42
  v43 code: GET user:123:v43   <- miss, fetch fresh
  + no stale data ever served
  + old keys expire naturally
  + no deploy-time flush needed

Fix 2: deploy-triggered flush
  deploy pipeline:
    1. deploy new code (dark, not receiving traffic)
    2. FLUSHDB or DEL user:*
    3. warm cache (background fetch of hot keys)
    4. cut traffic over
  + simple, works for any change
  - brief stampede if not warmed
```

### Q4. You have a multi-region deployment. The US-East cache and EU-West cache both have TTL=60s for the same key. Users in different regions see different values for up to 60s. How do you make this consistent?
**Answer:** Two layers of fix. (1) **Global origin with regional caches**: both regional caches fetch from the same global origin (database or primary cache), so they eventually converge to the same value within one TTL window (60s). The inconsistency window is bounded by the TTL — users in different regions may see different values, but only for up to 60s after a write. (2) **Cross-region invalidation**: when a write happens in one region, it sends an invalidation event to the other region's cache (via a pub/sub channel, a CDC stream, or a global Redis instance). The other region's cache evicts the key immediately, and the next read fetches the fresh value from the global origin. This shrinks the inconsistency window from 60s to the propagation latency of the invalidation (typically <1s for pub/sub). The trade-off: invalidation adds infrastructure (a pub/sub channel) and complexity (handling lost/duplicate events). Most teams accept the TTL-bounded inconsistency for routine updates and reserve cross-region invalidation for high-priority writes (e.g., a user deleting their account should be visible globally within seconds). Real-world: Netflix's EVCache does cross-region invalidation via a Kafka-based event bus; Cloudflare's cache uses a global purge API that propagates to all POPs within seconds; Discord uses Redis pub/sub for cross-shard invalidation. The pattern: TTL for routine freshness, explicit invalidation for must-be-consistent writes.
**Visual:**
```
Before (TTL only, no invalidation):
  US-East write: user:123 = "Alice"
  US-East cache: user:123 = "Alice" (TTL=60s)
  EU-West cache: user:123 = "Bob"   (TTL=60s, stale)
  + inconsistency for up to 60s

After (TTL + cross-region invalidation):
  US-East write: user:123 = "Alice"
                + publish invalidation event
                                |
                                v
  EU-West cache: receive event, DEL user:123
                 next read: fetch "Alice" from global origin
  + inconsistency shrinks to <1s (event propagation latency)
  + routine updates still TTL-bounded (no invalidation needed)
```

### Q5. Your team uses a 24-hour TTL for a rarely-changing config object. After a config change, ops has to wait 24 hours for it to propagate, or manually flush the cache. How do you improve this workflow?
**Answer:** Add an event-driven invalidation alongside the long TTL. The long TTL is correct for routine reads (the config rarely changes, so a long TTL maximizes hit rate and minimizes backend load). The problem is propagating changes quickly. The fix: when the config is updated, the config service publishes an invalidation event (to a pub/sub topic, a CDC stream, or a webhook), and each cache subscriber evicts the key on receipt. The next read misses and fetches the fresh config. This gives the best of both worlds: 24-hour TTL for hit rate (the config is read thousands of times per second, so the cache absorbs 99.99% of reads), with sub-second propagation for changes (the invalidation event reaches all caches within ~1s). The implementation is small: a `DEL config:feature_flags` call in the event handler, plus the pub/sub plumbing. As a fallback (in case the event is lost), keep the 24-hour TTL — even if the invalidation fails, the config still propagates within 24 hours. Real-world: LaunchDarkly and other feature-flag services use streaming updates (WebSocket or SSE) to push config changes to clients in <1s, with a long TTL as a fallback; Spring Cloud Config uses a `/refresh` webhook that caches call to evict; Netflix's EVCache uses CDC events for config invalidation. The pattern: long TTL for hit rate + event-driven invalidation for fast propagation, with TTL as the safety net.
**Visual:**
```
Before (TTL=24h only):
  T=0     config change
  T=0-24h cache still serves old config
  ops: wait 24h, or manually FLUSHDB (risky)

After (TTL=24h + event invalidation):
  T=0       config service publishes invalidation event
  T=0.1     cache subscriber: DEL config:feature_flags
  T=0.2     next read: miss, fetch fresh config
  + propagation <1s (event latency)
  + hit rate unchanged (TTL still 24h for routine reads)
  + fallback: if event lost, TTL still propagates within 24h
```

### Q6. You're caching API responses from a third-party service that's rate-limited to 100 requests/second. The cache TTL is 10 seconds, but you're hitting the rate limit. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The TTL is too short for the request volume. If you have 1,000 QPS of reads and a 10-second TTL, you do 1,000 reads/s × 10s = 10,000 cache hits per TTL window, but only 1 miss per TTL window — so the cache should generate only 0.1 requests/s to the third party, well under the 100/s limit. If you're hitting the rate limit, something is causing extra misses. Likely causes: (1) The cache key isn't normalized — `GET /users/123` and `GET /users/123?` are cached as different keys, doubling misses. (2) The cache is being evicted by LRU before the TTL expires — capacity is too small for the working set. (3) Multiple cache instances (e.g., one per pod) each maintain their own cache, multiplying misses by the pod count. (4) The TTL is being applied inconsistently — some writes use TTL=10, others use TTL=0 (no cache). Fixes: (1) Normalize the cache key (strip trailing slashes, sort query params, lowercase headers). (2) Increase cache capacity or use a longer TTL. (3) Move to a shared cache (Redis) instead of per-pod in-process caches. (4) Audit every SET call to ensure consistent TTL. If the working set is genuinely too large for the rate limit (e.g., 1M unique keys, each accessed once per minute, TTL=60s means 1M/60 = 16,666 misses/s — far over the 100/s limit), you have to either reduce the working set (cache only hot keys, defer cold keys to the source) or negotiate a higher rate limit. Real-world: integrations with Stripe, Twilio, and Salesforce APIs routinely hit this; the fix is a shared Redis cache with careful key normalization and TTL tuning.
**Visual:**
```
Expected miss rate:
  1000 QPS reads, TTL=10s
  -> 1 miss per 10s = 0.1 misses/s
  -> well under 100/s rate limit

Actual: hitting rate limit, so misses are ~100x higher. Likely:
  (1) cache key not normalized:
      GET /users/123   and   GET /users/123?   -> 2 keys, 2 misses
  (2) per-pod caches (10 pods, each 0.1/s = 1/s, but warm-up misses)
  (3) LRU evicting before TTL (capacity too small)
  (4) inconsistent TTL (some writes use TTL=0)

Fixes:
  + normalize keys (strip ?, sort params, lowercase)
  + shared Redis cache (not per-pod)
  + capacity > working set, or longer TTL
  + audit every SET for consistent TTL
```

### Q7. Your application writes to the database and then writes to the cache with TTL=300s. Occasionally, users see stale data for the full 5 minutes after a write. What's the bug, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The bug is a race condition between the database write and the cache write. The sequence `1. write DB; 2. write cache` is not atomic: if another read happens between steps 1 and 2, it reads the old cache value (stale), fetches the new value from the DB (because the cache miss), and writes the new value to the cache — but then step 2 overwrites it with... wait, the issue is different. The actual race: `1. write DB; 2. write cache(V_new)` — but if step 2 happens before step 1 commits (or if a concurrent read fetches V_old from the DB after the write but before the cache write), the cache can be populated with V_old and stay stale for the full TTL. Fixes: (1) **Write-through with version check**: include a version (or timestamp) in the cache value; on read, if the cached version is older than the DB's, treat as a miss. (2) **Delayed double-write**: after writing the DB, sleep briefly (e.g., 100 ms) to let the DB replication lag settle, then write the cache. Ugly but pragmatic. (3) **Cache-aside with read-repair**: don't write the cache on DB write at all; let the next read miss and fetch fresh. The cache stays stale only until the next read, not for the full TTL. (4) **CDC-driven invalidation**: the DB's binlog publishes an invalidation event after the commit; the cache evicts on receipt. This is the most robust: the invalidation happens after the DB commit, so there's no race. Real-world: Facebook's TAO uses CDC-driven invalidation; Netflix's EVCache uses a similar pattern; the cache-aside pattern (don't write cache on DB write) is the simplest and avoids the race entirely. The root cause: mixing synchronous cache writes with asynchronous DB replication creates a window where the cache can be populated with stale data; the fix is to either not write the cache on DB write (cache-aside) or to invalidate via a post-commit signal (CDC).
**Visual:**
```
Bug: race between DB write and cache write
  T=0   thread A: write DB (V_new)
  T=0.1 thread B: read cache -> miss
  T=0.2 thread B: read DB -> V_new (DB has committed)
  T=0.3 thread B: write cache(V_new)
  T=0.4 thread A: write cache(V_old)  <- BUG: A read V_old before its DB commit
  T=0.5 - T=300: cache serves V_old (stale for full TTL)

Fix 1: cache-aside (don't write cache on DB write)
  T=0   thread A: write DB (V_new)   (don't touch cache)
  T=0.1 thread B: read cache -> miss -> fetch V_new -> write cache(V_new)
  + no race, cache populated by next read with fresh data
  + cache stays stale only until next read, not for full TTL

Fix 2: CDC-driven invalidation
  T=0   thread A: write DB (V_new)
  T=0.1 binlog publishes invalidation event
  T=0.2 cache evicts key (after DB commit, no race)
  T=0.3 next read: miss -> fetch V_new -> write cache(V_new)
```
